title: Pescatarian Dinner Ideas: 8 Easy Weeknight Fish Dinners
meta_description: Eight easy pescatarian dinners from fresh or frozen salmon, cod, shrimp, trout and scallops, mostly one pan, with USDA protein numbers and lemon, not salt.
excerpt: Eight easy weeknight dinners from fresh or frozen fish and shellfish, most of them one pan, plus quick lunches from the leftovers.
author: sarah
content:
It's 5 o'clock, you're tired, and there's a bag of frozen cod in the freezer and no plan. I know that moment well. I cook for one most nights now, and the dinners that actually get made on a Tuesday are the ones with five ingredients and one pan.

These pescatarian dinner ideas are built for exactly that night. Eight easy dinners from fresh or frozen fish and shellfish, most of them one pan and quick enough for a weeknight. If you'd like to see how a fish dinner fits your own calorie and protein numbers, the free PescoDial calculator gives you a starting point from your age, height and weight.

The weeknight formula

Think in a pattern, not recipes. Every dinner below has three parts.

  • A palm-sized piece of fish or shellfish. The American Heart Association counts a serving as 3 ounces cooked, or about three quarters of a cup of flaked fish, and recommends 2 servings of fish a week, particularly fatty fish.
  • A vegetable that cooks in the same time. Green beans, broccoli, zucchini, spinach, cherry tomatoes.
  • Flavour from acid and herbs, not salt. Lemon, garlic, dill, paprika, black pepper.

Fish is done at 145°F in the thickest part, or when the flesh is no longer see-through and separates easily with a fork. Shrimp and scallops are done when they turn pearly and opaque. A cheap instant-read thermometer ends the guessing.

Every fish on this page is on the FDA and EPA "Best Choices" list, the lowest-mercury group. Our guide to low-mercury fish has the full list.

Watch the salt in the sauce

Most plain fish is low in sodium. A 3-ounce piece of cooked Atlantic salmon has about 50 mg. Scallops run higher, about 570 mg per 3 ounces cooked, so they need no salt at all. The sauce is where dinner quietly turns salty. One tablespoon of regular soy sauce carries about 880 mg, and a tablespoon of bottled teriyaki sauce about 690 mg. The Dietary Guidelines advise less than 2,300 mg for the whole day.

If you take medicine: these are everyday dinners, but a few medicines are worth a quick conversation first. If you take blood-pressure medicine, the salt in sauces and seasoning blends is the part to ask about. If you're on a blood thinner such as warfarin, the spinach and other leafy greens here carry vitamin K, and the amount you eat each day matters. If you take diabetes medicine, changing the rice, potatoes or tortillas on your plate can change how your blood sugar runs. If you take a statin, the same applies: ask your doctor or pharmacist before you change anything. This is not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicine.

So these recipes use reduced-sodium soy sauce, measured, not poured, and spice blends mixed at home with no salt. Nothing gets salted on top.

8 easy weeknight fish dinners

1. Sheet-pan salmon and green beans

Toss a big handful of green beans with a teaspoon of olive oil on a sheet pan and roast at 425°F for 8 minutes. Push them aside, add a salmon fillet, top with lemon slices and dill, and roast until it flakes and reaches 145°F. One pan to wash.

2. Cod baked in tomatoes and garlic

Simmer a can of no-salt-added diced tomatoes with two sliced garlic cloves and a pinch of chili flakes in an oven-safe skillet. Nestle in a cod or haddock fillet, cover, and bake until the fish is opaque. Top with parsley.

3. Shrimp and broccoli stir-fry

Stir-fry broccoli in a little oil for 3 minutes, add peeled shrimp, garlic and grated ginger, and cook until the shrimp turn pink and curl. Finish with one teaspoon of reduced-sodium soy sauce and a squeeze of lime.

4. Pan-seared trout with herbs and potatoes

Trout fillets are thin, so they cook in about 3 minutes a side in a hot cast iron pan. Start halved baby potatoes in the microwave first, then crisp them in the same pan. Finish with lemon, parsley and black pepper.

5. Fish tacos with pollock or tilapia

Rub frozen-then-thawed pollock or tilapia with cumin, smoked paprika and garlic powder, then pan-cook until it flakes. Pile into corn tortillas with shredded cabbage, sliced avocado and a spoon of plain Greek yogurt stirred with lime juice. Skip the packet taco seasoning: USDA puts two teaspoons of the dry mix at about 410 mg of sodium.

6. Seared scallops with garlic spinach

Pat the scallops very dry, which is the whole secret to a golden crust. Sear in a hot pan with a little oil, about 2 minutes a side, and set aside. Wilt two big handfuls of spinach with garlic in the same pan. Add lemon and you're done.

7. Blackened catfish with crunchy slaw

Mix your own blackening spice: paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, thyme, black pepper and a pinch of cayenne, no salt. Coat catfish fillets and cook in a hot skillet until dark and flaky. Serve with shredded cabbage tossed in vinegar and a drizzle of olive oil.

8. Lemon-dill haddock in foil

Lay a haddock or cod fillet on a sheet of foil with sliced zucchini, cherry tomatoes, lemon slices and dill. Fold into a packet and bake until the fish flakes. The steam keeps lean white fish moist.

The dinner table

Protein is per 3-ounce cooked serving of the fish alone, so you can match it to your calculator numbers.

2. Tomato-baked codCod (or haddock)19 g (haddock 17 g)
3. Shrimp stir-fryShrimp20 g
4. Pan-seared troutRainbow trout20 g
5. Fish tacosTilapia (or Alaska pollock)22 g (pollock 17 g)

Fresh or frozen?

Frozen is fine, and on a weeknight it's often better. It waits for you. I buy big bags of frozen cod and shrimp on my weekly shop.

  • Thaw it right. Overnight in the fridge, or sealed in a plastic bag and set in cold water if you're in a hurry.
  • Read the bag. Some frozen shrimp and fish are treated to hold moisture. USDA lists cooked shrimp with these additives at about 800 mg of sodium per 3 ounces, against about 95 mg for plain cooked shrimp. Compare the sodium line on two brands.
  • Skip the breaded kind most nights. It brings extra sodium and refined flour.

Pantry cans count too, they're just a different page. For sardine and canned salmon meals, see our canned fish recipes.

Pescatarian lunch ideas from last night's dinner

Cooking for one taught me this: make two portions and lunch is already done. Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 to 4 days.

  • Flake leftover salmon over greens with cucumber, a few olives and lemon-olive oil dressing.
  • Fold leftover shrimp stir-fry into a whole-grain wrap with extra cabbage.
  • Turn the last of the blackened catfish into a grain bowl with brown rice and slaw.

A note on fish and shellfish allergies

Fish and crustacean shellfish, such as shrimp, are on the FDA's list of nine major food allergens, listed as two separate allergens. If you're allergic to either, skip those dinners.

When to talk to your doctor

Get care if you notice any of these:

  • Hives, itching, a tingling mouth, stomach cramps or vomiting soon after eating fish or shellfish, even if it passes.
  • Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or feeling faint after eating seafood. That's an emergency: call 911 or your local emergency number.
  • Shakiness, sweating or confusion after a lighter dinner, especially if you take diabetes medicine. These can be signs of low blood sugar.
  • Unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums if you take a blood thinner.
  • New swelling in your ankles or legs, or home blood pressure readings that keep running above the target your doctor gave you.

The bottom line

Fish, a vegetable that cooks alongside it, and lemon instead of salt. Pick three of these dinners, keep frozen fish on hand, and cook double so lunch is done.
